school-primary-english.title: Pathshala Primary English (Class 1–5)
school-primary-english.description: From phonics to confident reading and writing: sounds, sight words, grammar, vocabulary, comprehension and writing for Class 1–5.

courses.title: Class 1 English: Sounds, words and first sentences
courses.summary: Learn letter sounds, blend them into short words, read common sight words, and write your first sentences with a capital letter and a full stop.
outcomes: Learners can say the main sound of each letter
Learners can blend sounds to read 3-letter words like cat, pen, sun
Learners can read and spell common sight words
Learners can write a short sentence with a capital letter and a full stop
Learners can use 'a' and 'an' correctly with naming words

scenes.text: Aarav, 6, lives in Nagpur. He knows the alphabet song but cannot read signs yet.
His mother points to the letter **s** and hisses like a snake: 'sss'.
'Every letter has a name and a sound,' she says. 'The name is "ess", the sound is "sss".'
Next day, Aarav sees STOP on a road sign and sounds it out: s-t-o-p. 'Stop!' He reads his first word.

steps.title: Letter names and letter sounds
steps.body:
Each letter has a **name** (what we sing in the ABC song) and a **sound** (what it says in words). For reading, the **sound** matters most.

- **s** says /s/ as in *sun*
- **a** says /a/ as in *ant*
- **t** says /t/ as in *tap*
- **p** says /p/ as in *pan*
- **i** says /i/ as in *ink*
- **n** says /n/ as in *net*
steps.say: Each letter has a name and a sound.

steps.title: Vowels and consonants
steps.body:
Five letters are **vowels**: **a, e, i, o, u**. Every word needs at least one vowel sound (sometimes **y** helps too, as in *my*).

The other letters are **consonants**: b, c, d, f, g, …

steps.title: Short vowel sounds
steps.body:
- a — *apple*, *cat*
- e — *egg*, *pen*
- i — *igloo*, *pin*
- o — *orange* (in many accents), *dog*
- u — *umbrella*, *sun*

steps.title: Capital and small letters
steps.body: Each letter has a **capital** (A, B, C) and a **small** form (a, b, c). Most words in books use small letters. Capitals start names and sentences.

steps.title: Common mix-ups: b and d, p and q
steps.body: **b** has its tummy on the right (like a bat then a ball: | then o). **d** has its tummy on the left (a drum then a stick: o then |). Make a 'bed' with your fists: left thumb up = b, right thumb up = d.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find 5 things at home and say their first sound: *fan* /f/, *mug* /m/, *bag* /b/, *lock* /l/, *tap* /t/.

quiz.q: Which word starts with the sound /m/?
Which of these is a vowel?
quiz.why: The vowels are a, e, i, o, u.

quiz.q: What is the first sound in 'dog'?
Which is the capital form of 'g'?
Which word starts with a vowel?
quiz.why: Egg begins with e, a vowel.

scenes.text: Zara in Toronto and her cousin Kiara in Delhi video-call every Sunday.
They play 'robot talk': Zara says 'c-a-t' in a robot voice.
Kiara pushes the sounds together faster: 'c-a-t… cat!'
Then Kiara says 'p-i-g', 's-u-n', 'h-e-n'. Both cousins read every word.

steps.title: Blending
steps.body:
**Blending** means saying each sound and then joining them smoothly into a word.

- c — a — t → **cat**
- p — i — g → **pig**
- s — u — n → **sun**

Say the sounds faster and faster until they join.

steps.title: Word families
steps.body:
Words that end the same way rhyme and form a **family**:

- **-at**: cat, bat, hat, mat, rat, sat
- **-en**: hen, pen, ten, men
- **-ig**: big, dig, pig, wig
- **-op**: hop, mop, top, pop
- **-ug**: bug, hug, jug, mug, rug

steps.title: Segmenting for spelling
steps.body: To **spell**, do the opposite: break the word into sounds and write a letter for each. *dog* → d / o / g. Tap a finger for each sound.

steps.title: Common mistake: adding 'uh'
steps.body: Say /m/ as 'mmm', not 'muh'. If you say 'cuh-a-tuh', it sounds like 'cuhatuh', not *cat*. Keep sounds short and clean.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Change one letter to make a new word: cat → hat → hot → hop → top → tip. How long a chain can you make?

activity.prompt: Blend the sounds and write the word.

quiz.q: Change the first letter of 'mug' to make a word for an insect.
What is the middle sound in 'pin'?

lessons.title: Sight words and my first sentences

scenes.text: Every morning, Grandma Fatima in Hyderabad sticks a note on the fridge for Sami.
Today it says: **I like the red apple.**
Sami can sound out *red* but 'the' doesn't sound like t-h-e. Grandma says, 'Some words we just learn by sight.'
Sami writes back: **I love you.** — with a capital I and a full stop.

steps.title: Sight words
steps.body:
Some very common words don't follow simple sound rules, so we learn them **by sight**: *the, is, a, I, to, was, said, you, are, he, she, we, my, of, they, have, come, here*.

These words appear in almost every sentence, so knowing them makes reading quick.

steps.title: What a sentence is
steps.body:
A **sentence** is a group of words that makes **complete sense**.

- ✅ *The cat is on the mat.*
- ❌ *on the mat* (we don't know what is on the mat)

Every sentence starts with a **capital letter** and ends with a **full stop (.)**, a question mark (?) or an exclamation mark (!).

steps.title: Building a sentence
steps.body:
Who? → *Sami*
Does what? → *eats*
What? → *a mango*

**Sami eats a mango.** The word **I** is always a capital, even in the middle: *Mum and I play.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the full stop.
- Writing 'i' instead of 'I'.
- Leaving no space between words: *Ilikemilk* → *I like milk.* Put a finger space between words.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write 3 sentences about your family: *My mum is kind. My brother likes cricket. I have a cat.*

activity.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.

quiz.why: It makes complete sense and has a capital and full stop.

quiz.q: Which should always be a capital letter?
quiz.why: The word I is always a capital.
Capital at the start, full stop at the end.
'The' is learned by sight; the others can be sounded out.

scenes.text: In Ms Kapoor's Class 1 in Shimla, there's a lost-and-found box.
Inside: a cap, an umbrella, a bottle, an orange, a book.
Tenzin asks, 'Why do we say *an* umbrella but *a* cap?'
Ms Kapoor: 'Listen to the first **sound**. If it's a vowel sound, use **an**.'

steps.title: Naming words (nouns)
steps.body:
A **naming word** (noun) names a **person, place, animal or thing**.

- Person: *teacher, Tenzin, doctor*
- Place: *school, Shimla, park*
- Animal: *dog, yak, parrot*
- Thing: *cap, book, umbrella*

steps.title: Special names
steps.body: Names of particular people and places start with a **capital letter**: *Tenzin, Ms Kapoor, India, Shimla, Monday*. These are **proper nouns**.

steps.title: a or an?
steps.body:
Use **an** before a word that starts with a **vowel sound**; use **a** before a consonant sound.

- **an** apple, **an** egg, **an** ink pot, **an** orange, **an** umbrella
- **a** cap, **a** bottle, **a** dog, **a** book

steps.title: Listen to the sound, not just the letter
steps.body: We say **an hour** (the h is silent, it starts with an 'ow' sound) and **a uniform** (it starts with a 'yoo' sound). The rule is about the **sound**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Look around your room and name 5 nouns with a or an: *a fan, an eraser, a bed, an almirah, a window*.

activity.prompt: Does it take 'a' or 'an'?

quiz.why: Elephant starts with a vowel sound.
Banana starts with a consonant sound.
Delhi is the name of a particular place.
The h is silent, so it starts with a vowel sound.

questions.q: What is the first sound in 'fish'?

questions.why: Owl starts with a vowel sound.

questions.q: Which is a naming word for a person?
Which group has only naming words?
Which word does NOT belong to the -ug family?
Change one letter of 'cat' to make a word for a baby's bed.

courses.title: Class 2 English: Phonics power, nouns, verbs & reading
courses.summary: Read words with sh, ch, th and magic e, make plurals, use action words and is/am/are, and read a short story to answer questions about it.
outcomes: Learners can read and spell words with digraphs (sh, ch, th, ck, ng) and long vowels with magic e
Learners can change singular nouns to plurals with -s, -es and common irregular forms
Learners can identify verbs and choose is, am or are
Learners can answer who/what/where/why questions about a short passage

lessons.title: Two letters, one sound — and magic e

scenes.text: Rohit and his friend Chloe walk past a shop in Mysuru with a sign: **SHOES & CHAPPALS**.
Rohit reads s-h-o-e-s… 'Sss-hoes?'
Chloe laughs: 'S and h together make one sound: **sh**! Shoes!'
At home Rohit finds more: *ship, chip, thin, duck, ring* — and learns about **magic e** that turns *cap* into *cape*.

steps.title: Digraphs: two letters, one sound
steps.body:
- **sh** — *ship, fish, shop*
- **ch** — *chair, lunch, chips*
- **th** — *thin, three, this, mother*
- **ck** — *duck, sock, back* (at the end of short words)
- **ng** — *ring, sing, king*
- **wh** — *when, what, whale*

steps.title: Magic e (silent e)
steps.body:
A silent **e** at the end makes the vowel say its **name** (long sound).

- cap → **cape**
- kit → **kite**
- hop → **hope**
- cut → **cute**
- pet → **Pete**

The e itself is silent.

steps.title: Vowel teams
steps.body: Two vowels together often make one long sound: **ee** (*tree, see*), **ea** (*leaf, sea*), **ai** (*rain, train*), **oa** (*boat, coat*). A handy hint: 'When two vowels go walking, the first one often does the talking' — but it does not always work (*bread*, *said*).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading *sh* as s + h.
- Writing *kit* when you mean *kite* — say the word: long 'i' needs the magic e.
- Writing *duk* instead of *duck* — short vowel + /k/ at the end is usually **ck**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Read aloud and sort: *ship, chin, thumb, bake, home, rain, boat*. Which have a digraph, which have magic e, which have a vowel team?

activity.prompt: Add magic e: match each short word to its new word.

quiz.q: What does magic e do to 'kit'?
quiz.why: The i says its name: kite.
Short vowel + /k/ at the end: ck.

quiz.q: Which word has a long 'a' sound?
quiz.why: ai in rain makes the long a.
Th-umb: t and h together make one sound.

scenes.text: Aunty Grace sells vegetables in Shillong market. Her nephew Ben writes the price board.
He writes: *tomatos, potatos, carrots, leafs*.
Aunty Grace laughs: 'Two of those are right!'
She teaches him plural rules, and he fixes it: *tomatoes, potatoes, carrots, leaves*.

steps.title: Singular and plural
steps.body: **Singular** = one (*a carrot*). **Plural** = more than one (*carrots*). Most nouns just add **-s**: *book → books, girl → girls, tree → trees*.

steps.title: Add -es
steps.body:
Add **-es** after **s, ss, sh, ch, x** (and many words ending in **o**):

- bus → buses, glass → glasses, dish → dishes, watch → watches, box → boxes
- tomato → tomatoes, potato → potatoes, mango → mangoes (mangos is also seen)
- but photo → photos, piano → pianos

steps.title: y and f endings
steps.body:
- Consonant + **y** → change y to **ies**: baby → babies, city → cities.
- Vowel + y → just add s: toy → toys, day → days.
- Many **f / fe** words → **ves**: leaf → leaves, knife → knives, wolf → wolves (but roof → roofs).

steps.title: Irregular plurals
steps.body: Some plurals don't follow rules — learn them: man → **men**, woman → **women**, child → **children**, tooth → **teeth**, foot → **feet**, mouse → **mice**. Some stay the same: sheep → **sheep**, deer → **deer**, fish → usually **fish**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: *childs, foots, mouses, sheeps* are all wrong. Also, don't use an apostrophe for plurals: *apple's for sale* ❌ → *apples for sale* ✅.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a shopping list with plurals: 3 (mango), 2 (box) of sweets, 6 (egg), 2 (loaf) of bread.

activity.prompt: Write the plural.
activity.text: one box, two ___ ; one baby, two ___ ; one leaf, two ___ ; one child, two ___ ; one toy, two ___

lessons.title: Doing words and is / am / are

scenes.text: At sports day in Kochi, Class 2 takes turns being the commentator.
Anil: 'Meera **runs** fast! The boys **jumps** high!'
Everyone giggles. Ms D'Souza helps: 'The boys **jump** high.'
By the end, Anil says: 'I **am** tired. We **are** happy. Meera **is** the winner!'

steps.title: Verbs are doing (action) words
steps.body:
A **verb** tells what someone or something **does**: *run, jump, eat, sing, write, sleep, think*.

In *The dog barks*, **barks** is the verb. Every sentence needs a verb.

steps.title: Being verbs: am, is, are
steps.body:
- **I am** (only with I)
- **He / she / it is**, and one person or thing: *Meera is*, *the cat is*
- **We / you / they are**, and more than one: *the boys are*

*I am six. She is kind. They are friends.*

steps.title: One does, many do
steps.body:
With one person or thing (not I or you), the action word usually takes **-s**:

- *Meera runs.* *The bird sings.*
- *The girls run.* *Birds sing.* *I run.* *You run.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *I is happy* ❌ → *I am happy* ✅
- *They is late* ❌ → *They are late* ✅
- *He go to school* ❌ → *He goes to school* ✅

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Watch your family for 2 minutes and write 4 sentences: *Papa reads. Mummy cooks. My sisters play. I am writing.*

statements.why: Happy describes a feeling; it is an adjective.

quiz.q: Find the verb: 'The baby sleeps in the cot.'
quiz.why: Sleeps is what the baby does.

lessons.title: Reading a story and answering questions

story.title: Pinky the kitten (a story to read)

scenes.text: Pinky was a small white kitten who lived in a bakery in Pune.
One rainy day, Pinky ran outside after a butterfly and could not find her way back. She hid under a parked scooter, wet and cold.
A girl named Nisha heard a tiny 'meow'. She saw the bakery's name on Pinky's collar tag.
Nisha carried Pinky to the bakery. The baker, Mr Joshi, was so happy that he gave Nisha a warm bun. From then on, Pinky stayed inside when it rained.

steps.title: Read twice
steps.body: First read the story for fun. Then read it again **slowly**, looking for details: **who**, **where**, **when**, **what happened**, **why** and **how it ended**.

steps.title: Question words
steps.body:
- **Who** → a person or animal (*Pinky, Nisha, Mr Joshi*)
- **Where** → a place (*a bakery in Pune; under a scooter*)
- **When** → a time (*one rainy day*)
- **What** → a thing or event (*she chased a butterfly*)
- **Why** → a reason (*Nisha knew where to go because of the collar tag*)

steps.title: Find the answer in the text
steps.body:
Q: Why did Pinky get lost?
Look for the part about leaving: *'Pinky ran outside after a butterfly and could not find her way back.'*
A: **Pinky got lost because she chased a butterfly.** Answer in a full sentence.

steps.title: Thinking questions
steps.body: Some answers are not written directly. *How did Mr Joshi feel?* The story says he was 'so happy', and he gave a gift. *What lesson did Pinky learn?* To stay inside when it rains. Use clues + your own thinking.

steps.title: Common mistake: guessing without reading
steps.body: Don't answer from memory or imagination. Go back to the text and **point** to the words that prove your answer.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Retell Pinky's story to someone at home in 4 sentences: beginning, problem, help, ending.

items.back: She ran outside after a butterfly.

items.front: How did Nisha know where Pinky lived?
items.back: The bakery's name was on her collar tag.
Mr Joshi gave Nisha a bun, and Pinky stayed inside when it rained.

quiz.q: What was the weather when Pinky got lost?

quiz.why: She hid under a parked scooter.

quiz.q: What did Mr Joshi give Nisha?
quiz.why: He gave her a warm bun.
She helped a lost kitten home.

quiz.q: Which question word asks for a reason?

questions.q: Find the verb: 'Ravi kicks the ball.'
Which question word asks about a place?
In the story, why did Pinky stay inside when it rained afterwards?
options: She had learned from getting lost
questions.why: This is a thinking question: she learned from the rainy-day adventure.

courses.title: Class 3 English: Pronouns, describing words, tenses & punctuation
courses.summary: Use pronouns and adjectives, tell what is happening now and what happened yesterday, punctuate sentences correctly, and grow vocabulary with synonyms, antonyms and homophones.
outcomes: Learners can replace nouns with the right pronouns
Learners can use adjectives, including comparing forms (tall, taller, tallest)
Learners can write sentences in simple present and simple past, including common irregular verbs
Learners can use capital letters, full stops, question marks, exclamation marks, commas and apostrophes
Learners can use synonyms, antonyms and common homophones correctly

scenes.text: Ishita in Varanasi writes to Grandpa: 'Ishita went to the park. Ishita saw a dog. The dog was big. The dog licked Ishita.'
Grandpa writes back: 'Lovely! But why so many Ishitas and dogs?'
Ishita rewrites: '**I** went to the park. **I** saw a **huge, fluffy** dog. **It** licked **me**!'
Pronouns stopped the repeating, and adjectives made the picture clear.

steps.title: Pronouns replace nouns
steps.body:
A **pronoun** stands in for a noun so we don't repeat it.

- I / me, we / us
- you
- he / him, she / her, it
- they / them

*Rahul is tall. **He** plays basketball.* *The books are new. **They** are on the desk.*

steps.title: I or me?
steps.body:
Use **I** when you do the action, **me** when the action is done to you.

- ***I** kicked the ball.* *The dog licked **me**.*
- *Mum and **I** went shopping.* (Test: remove 'Mum and' → '**I** went shopping' ✓)
- *Grandpa gave sweets to Asha and **me**.* (→ 'gave sweets to **me**' ✓)

steps.title: Adjectives describe nouns
steps.body:
An **adjective** tells **what kind, how many, which one** or **what colour**: *huge, fluffy, three, red, kind, noisy*.

*a **noisy** market*, *two **ripe** mangoes*, *the **brave** girl*.

steps.title: Comparing
steps.body:
- Short adjectives: **tall → taller → tallest**, **big → bigger → biggest**, **happy → happier → happiest**.
- Longer adjectives: **beautiful → more beautiful → most beautiful**.
- Irregular: **good → better → best**, **bad → worse → worst**.

Use *-er / more* for **two** things and *-est / most* for **three or more**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *Me and Sita went* ❌ → *Sita and I went* ✅ (it is polite to put yourself last, too)
- *more taller* ❌ → *taller* ✅
- *gooder* ❌ → *better* ✅

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Describe your best friend in 3 sentences using at least 4 adjectives and 2 pronouns.

activity.prompt: Is it a pronoun or an adjective?

quiz.q: 'Rohan and Ali are friends. ___ play together.'
Find the adjective: 'The tired farmer sat down.'
This is the ___ mango in the basket.

lessons.title: Now and yesterday: present and past tense

scenes.text: Kavya from Bhopal keeps a holiday diary in Singapore with her cousin Wei Ling.
Monday: 'Today we **visit** the zoo. A lion **sleeps** in the sun.'
On Tuesday she reads Monday's entry again and changes it: 'Yesterday we **visited** the zoo. A lion **slept** in the sun.'
Wei Ling says, 'Your verbs time-travelled!'

steps.title: Simple present
steps.body:
Use the **simple present** for habits, facts and things true now.

- *I **walk** to school every day.*
- *The sun **rises** in the east.*
- *She **likes** dosa.* (he / she / it → add **-s** or **-es**: go → goes, watch → watches)

steps.title: Simple past — regular verbs
steps.body:
For finished actions, most verbs add **-ed**: *walk → walked, play → played, jump → jumped*.

- Ends in e → add **d**: *dance → danced*
- Short verb ending consonant-vowel-consonant → double the last letter: *stop → stopped, hop → hopped*
- Consonant + y → **ied**: *cry → cried, carry → carried*

steps.title: Irregular past verbs
steps.body:
Many common verbs change completely. Learn these:

- go → **went**, come → **came**, see → **saw**, eat → **ate**
- sleep → **slept**, run → **ran**, write → **wrote**, take → **took**
- buy → **bought**, think → **thought**, have → **had**, is/am → **was**, are → **were**
- put → **put**, cut → **cut** (no change!)

steps.title: Time clue words
steps.body:
- Present: *every day, always, usually, often, now (with -ing)*
- Past: *yesterday, last week, in 2020, ago, this morning (if it's over)*

*Last Sunday we **went** to the beach.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *goed, eated, buyed* ❌ → *went, ate, bought* ✅
- *Yesterday I go* ❌ → *Yesterday I went* ✅
- *He go to school* ❌ → *He goes* ✅

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write 5 sentences about what you did last weekend. Underline every past-tense verb.

activity.prompt: Write the past tense.
activity.text: Yesterday I ___ (go) to the market. We ___ (buy) apples. My brother ___ (eat) two. Then it ___ (start) to rain and we ___ (run) home.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the past?

scenes.text: Tom in London texts his friend Arjun in Mumbai: 'Lets eat grandma'
Arjun replies: 'You're going to eat your grandma?!'
Tom: 'No! **Let's eat, Grandma!** I'm calling her to dinner!'
One comma and one apostrophe changed everything.

steps.title: End marks
steps.body:
- **Full stop (.)** ends a telling sentence: *I like rain.*
- **Question mark (?)** ends a question: *Do you like rain?*
- **Exclamation mark (!)** shows strong feeling: *What a storm!*

steps.title: Capital letters
steps.body: Use capitals for: the **first word** of a sentence, the word **I**, **names** of people, places, days, months, festivals and languages (*Priya, Kerala, Monday, July, Eid, Diwali, Christmas, Tamil*).

steps.title: Commas
steps.body:
- In a **list**: *I bought rice, dal, onions and tomatoes.*
- Before a **name** when talking to someone: *Let's eat, Grandma.*
- After *Yes / No*: *Yes, I can.*

steps.title: Apostrophes
steps.body:
1. **Short forms** (contractions): *do not → don't, I am → I'm, it is → it's, let us → let's*. The apostrophe replaces missing letters.
2. **Belonging**: *Riya's bag* (the bag of Riya), *the dog's bone*.

**its** (no apostrophe) = belonging to it: *The cat licked its paw.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *it's* vs *its*: *It's raining* (it is), *its tail*.
- Apostrophes are not for plurals: *banana's* ❌ → *bananas* ✅.
- Forgetting the ? on a question.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Fix this: *on monday rahul and i went to delhi did you go* → *On Monday, Rahul and I went to Delhi. Did you go?*

statements.s: 'Where is my pen?' needs a question mark.
'The cat licked it's paw' is correct.
'diwali' should start with a capital letter.
'I bought apple's' is correct for more than one apple.

quiz.why: It is → It's, capital at start, full stop.

quiz.q: Where does the comma go? 'Yes I can come.'

scenes.text: In a library in Kolkata, Ananya, Diego and Fatima start a 'Word Detective Club'.
Diego: 'Happy is boring. What else?' Ananya: '**Joyful, cheerful, glad, delighted**!'
Fatima: 'And the opposite? **Sad, unhappy, gloomy**.'
Then they find sound-alike pairs: *see / sea, hear / here, two / to / too*. 'Same sound, different meaning!'

steps.title: Synonyms: similar meaning
steps.body:
**Synonyms** are words with the same or nearly the same meaning.

- big — large, huge, enormous
- small — little, tiny
- fast — quick, rapid
- say — tell, speak, shout, whisper (each has a slightly different shade)

steps.title: Antonyms: opposite meaning
steps.body:
**Antonyms** are opposites: *hot ↔ cold, up ↔ down, early ↔ late, kind ↔ cruel*.

Some are made with prefixes: *happy ↔ **un**happy, possible ↔ **im**possible, honest ↔ **dis**honest*.

steps.title: Homophones: sound the same
steps.body:
- **see** (with eyes) / **sea** (ocean)
- **hear** (with ears) / **here** (this place)
- **two** (2) / **to** (towards) / **too** (also, or very)
- **their** (belonging to them) / **there** (that place) / **they're** (they are)
- **write** / **right**, **one** / **won**, **flour** / **flower**

steps.title: Use a dictionary
steps.body: Words in a dictionary are in **alphabetical order**. If the first letters are the same, look at the second letter: *ant, apple, axe*. A thesaurus lists synonyms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *Their going to school* ❌ → *They're going* ✅
- *I want to come to* ❌ → *I want to come too* ✅

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Replace 'nice' in these: *a nice day* (sunny), *a nice cake* (delicious), *a nice friend* (kind).

activity.prompt: Match each word to its opposite (antonym).

quiz.why: Huge and enormous both mean very big.

courses.title: Class 4 English: Reading deeply and writing well
courses.summary: Read passages with understanding (finding facts, guessing meanings, inferring), use adverbs, prepositions and conjunctions, write strong paragraphs, and write friendly letters and messages.
outcomes: Learners can find facts, work out word meanings from context and make inferences
Learners can use adverbs, prepositions and conjunctions to add detail and join ideas
Learners can plan and write a paragraph with a topic sentence, supporting details and a closing sentence
Learners can write an informal letter, a message and a polite email
Learners can check their own writing for capitals, punctuation and spelling

story.title: The secret of the stepwell (a passage)

scenes.text: Every summer, Manav visits his nani in a village near Jodhpur, where water is precious.

Nani takes him to an old **stepwell** — a deep well with hundreds of stone steps going down to the water. 'Long ago,' she says, 'people walked down these steps to fill their pots, even when the rains failed.'
At the bottom, the air is **cool**, though the sun outside is scorching. Manav notices carvings of dancers and elephants on the walls.
'Why did they make it so beautiful?' he asks. Nani smiles: 'Because water was a gift. People gathered here to talk, rest and celebrate.' Manav decides to write about it for his school magazine.

steps.title: Three kinds of questions
steps.body:
1. **Right there**: the answer is in the text. *What did people carry? — pots.*
2. **Think and search**: put together information from different sentences. *Why was the stepwell important? — water was scarce; people could reach water even when rains failed.*
3. **Inference (read between the lines)**: use clues + what you know. *How does Manav feel about the stepwell? — curious and impressed: he asks questions and decides to write about it.*

steps.title: Meaning from context
steps.body: Don't know a word? Use the sentence around it. *'the sun outside is **scorching**'* — the bottom is cool, *though* the sun is scorching, so scorching must mean **very hot**. Words like *though, but, because, so* give strong clues.

steps.title: Main idea vs details
steps.body: The **main idea** is what the whole passage is mostly about: *a stepwell was an important and beautiful place for water in a dry region.* **Details** support it: hundreds of steps, cool air, carvings.

steps.title: Before, during, after
steps.body:
- **Before**: read the title, guess what it's about.
- **During**: stop after each paragraph and say in your head what happened.
- **After**: retell the main idea in one sentence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Copying a whole paragraph as an answer. Pick only the part that answers the question.
- Answering inference questions with 'it doesn't say'. Look for clues!

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Read any newspaper article for children. Write its main idea in one sentence and two supporting details.

items.front: Right there: what did people carry down the steps?

items.back: Very hot — it is contrasted with the cool air at the bottom.

items.front: Think and search: why was the stepwell useful?
items.back: It let people reach water even when the rains failed, in a dry region.
Curious and impressed — he asks why it is beautiful and decides to write about it.
Stepwells were important, beautiful places that gave water and a gathering place in dry regions.

quiz.q: What does 'precious' most likely mean in 'water is precious'?
quiz.why: Water is scarce, so it is very valuable.

quiz.q: Which is an inference, not stated directly?
quiz.why: We work it out from his questions.

options: Stepwells were important for water and community
quiz.why: The passage is mostly about why stepwells mattered.

quiz.q: Which word is a context clue for 'scorching'?

scenes.text: At a birthday party in Bengaluru, Sophie and Kunal follow clues.
Clue 1: 'Walk **slowly** **towards** the big tree. Look **under** the blue mat.'
Clue 2: 'The prize is **behind** the door, **but** you must knock **politely** first!'
They find the treasure because they understood every little word.

steps.title: Adverbs tell how, when, where
steps.body:
An **adverb** adds information to a verb.

- **How**: slowly, quickly, politely, loudly, carefully (many end in -ly)
- **When**: now, soon, yesterday, early, later
- **Where**: here, there, outside, everywhere

*She sang **beautifully**.* *We will leave **soon**.*

steps.title: Prepositions show position
steps.body:
A **preposition** shows where or when something is, in relation to something else: **in, on, under, over, behind, between, beside, near, towards, through, at, by, during, after, before**.

*The cat is **under** the table.* *We play **after** school.*

steps.title: in, on, at for time
steps.body:
- **at** a clock time: *at 7 o'clock*
- **on** a day/date: *on Monday, on 15 August*
- **in** a month, year, season, part of day: *in July, in 2025, in winter, in the morning*

steps.title: Conjunctions join ideas
steps.body:
**Conjunctions** join words or sentences:

- **and** (adds): *I like tea and biscuits.*
- **but** (contrast): *It rained, but we played.*
- **or** (choice): *Tea or coffee?*
- **because** (reason): *I stayed home because I was ill.*
- **so** (result): *I was ill, so I stayed home.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *She sings good* ❌ → *She sings **well*** ✅ (well is the adverb of good)
- *on 7 o'clock* ❌ → *at 7 o'clock* ✅
- Starting with *because* without finishing: *Because it rained.* is not complete.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write directions from your room to the kitchen using 4 prepositions and 2 adverbs.

activity.prompt: Sort each word.

quiz.q: Find the adverb: 'The baby slept peacefully.'
I was hungry, ___ I ate a banana.
The ball is ___ the two boxes.

scenes.text: Ms Thomas in Thiruvananthapuram asks Class 4 to write about a favourite festival.
Ayaan writes: 'Onam is nice. I like it. It is nice. The end.'
Ms Thomas: 'Tell me **why** — what do you see, smell, taste, do?'
Ayaan rewrites with a topic sentence, three details and a closing line. The class claps.

steps.title: The parts of a paragraph
steps.body:
A paragraph is a group of sentences about **one** idea.

1. **Topic sentence** — tells the main idea: *Onam is my favourite festival because it brings my whole family together.*
2. **Supporting sentences** (3–5) — reasons, examples, details.
3. **Closing sentence** — wraps up: *That is why I wait all year for Onam.*

steps.title: A model paragraph
steps.body: *Onam is my favourite festival because it brings my whole family together. Early in the morning, my sister and I make a colourful pookalam of flowers at our door. At noon we sit on the floor and eat a sadya with many dishes served on a banana leaf. In the evening my cousins and I watch the boat race on TV and cheer loudly. That is why I wait all year for Onam.*

steps.title: Use the five senses
steps.body: Make writing come alive: what did you **see**, **hear**, **smell**, **taste**, **touch**? *The air smelled of jasmine. The drums thumped.* Use time words to order events: *first, next, then, after that, finally*.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Repeating the same word (*nice, nice, nice*). Use synonyms.
- Mixing two topics in one paragraph.
- Very long sentences joined with *and… and… and…*. Break them up.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a paragraph about your favourite food or game using the checklist below.

activity.prompt: Paragraph checklist — tick each one after you check your writing.
items: My first sentence tells the main idea (topic sentence)
I gave at least 3 details or reasons
I used at least one sense word (see, hear, smell, taste, touch)
I used order words like first, then, finally
I ended with a closing sentence
Every sentence starts with a capital and ends with . ? or !
I checked spellings of difficult words

quiz.q: What does a topic sentence do?
Which is the best topic sentence?
options: Cricket is my favourite game because it is exciting and teaches teamwork.
quiz.why: It states a clear idea with a reason.

quiz.q: Which order word fits the end?

scenes.text: Through a school exchange, Diya in Surat gets a pen pal: Lucas in São Paulo, Brazil.
Diya's first draft starts: 'hi lucas whats up' — no greeting line, no capital letters, no sign-off.
Her teacher shows her the parts of a friendly letter.
Diya sends a lovely letter about her city and asks Lucas questions. He writes back within a week.

steps.title: Parts of an informal (friendly) letter
steps.body:
1. **Your address and date** (top) — in emails the date appears automatically.
2. **Greeting**: *Dear Lucas,*
3. **Opening**: *I hope you are well. I am very happy to be your pen pal.*
4. **Body**: news, details, questions — one paragraph per topic.
5. **Closing**: *Please write back soon.*
6. **Sign-off**: *Your friend,* / *With love,* then your name.

steps.title: A short message
steps.body:
Messages are short and clear: **who** it is for, **what** happened, **who** it is from, **when**.

*Mum, Mrs Sen called at 4 p.m. The art class is moved to Friday. — Riya*

steps.title: A polite email
steps.body:
- **To**: the person's email address (check it carefully)
- **Subject**: short and clear — *Question about the science project*
- **Greeting**: *Dear Ms Rao,*
- **Body**: polite and to the point, with *please* and *thank you*
- **Sign-off**: *Thank you, Diya (Class 4B)*

steps.title: Safety and manners online
steps.body:
- Write to pen pals only through a school or parent-approved programme.
- **Never** share your home address, school name, phone number, passwords or photos with someone you only know online, without a parent's OK.
- Don't write in ALL CAPITALS — it looks like shouting.

choices.feedback: Polite and tells her who you are.

courses.title: Class 5 English: Grammar that grows, stories and poems
courses.summary: Master sentence types and subject–verb agreement, use continuous and perfect tenses, build vocabulary with prefixes, suffixes and idioms, enjoy poems, and plan and write your own stories.
outcomes: Learners can identify the four sentence types and the subject and predicate
Learners can use present/past continuous and present perfect, with correct subject–verb agreement
Learners can build word meanings from prefixes and suffixes and use common idioms
Learners can identify rhyme, rhythm, simile and metaphor in a poem
Learners can plan and write a story with a beginning, problem, climax and ending

scenes.text: Class 5 in Chandigarh runs a morning radio show. Harleen is the host.
'Good morning, everyone. **Did you finish your homework?** **Please switch off the fans when you leave.** **What a sunny day it is!**'
Her teacher points out that she used all four sentence types in a few seconds.
The class makes a game: spot the sentence type in every announcement.

steps.title: Four types of sentences
steps.body:
- **Statement (declarative)**: tells something. *The bus is late.*
- **Question (interrogative)**: asks. *Is the bus late?*
- **Command/request (imperative)**: tells someone to do something. *Please wait here.*
- **Exclamation (exclamatory)**: shows strong feeling. *What a long wait!*

steps.title: Subject and predicate
steps.body:
Every complete sentence has two parts:

- **Subject**: who or what the sentence is about — *The tall girl*
- **Predicate**: what the subject does or is — *won the race.*

In commands, the subject *you* is hidden: *(You) Close the door.*

steps.title: Finding them
steps.body:
- *My little brother | loves mangoes.*
- *The old banyan tree | fell in the storm.*
- *Priya and Sam | are best friends.*

Ask 'Who/what?' to find the subject and 'Does/is what?' for the predicate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A fragment like *Running in the park.* has no subject — add one: *The children were running in the park.*
- Two sentences squashed with a comma: *It rained, we stayed in.* → *It rained, so we stayed in.*

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write one sentence of each type about your school. Underline the subject in each statement.

activity.prompt: Sort by sentence type.

quiz.why: It asks someone to do something.

quiz.q: Subject of 'The hungry puppy ate quickly.'

options: The cat jumped over the wall.
quiz.why: It has a subject and predicate.

quiz.q: What is the hidden subject in 'Sit down.'?

lessons.title: Tenses that tell time, and agreement

scenes.text: Aisha in Mysuru Zoo sends voice notes to her grandfather in Dubai.
10:00: 'Nana, the giraffe **is eating** leaves right now!'
11:00: 'When we reached the lake, the ducks **were swimming**.'
12:00: 'I **have seen** 20 animals today! Each of them **is** amazing.'

steps.title: Continuous tenses
steps.body:
**Present continuous** — happening **now**: *am / is / are + verb-ing*.
*I **am reading**. She **is eating**. They **are playing**.*

**Past continuous** — was going on at a moment in the past: *was / were + verb-ing*.
*At 8 p.m. I **was sleeping**. The ducks **were swimming**.*

steps.title: Present perfect
steps.body:
Use **has / have + past participle** for something done at an unstated time up to now, or with results now.

- *I **have finished** my homework.* (so I can play)
- *She **has visited** Agra twice.*

Common past participles: *seen, eaten, gone, written, done, taken, been*. Don't use it with exact past times: *I have seen him yesterday* ❌ → *I saw him yesterday* ✅.

steps.title: Subject–verb agreement
steps.body:
Singular subject → singular verb; plural subject → plural verb.

- *The boy **runs**.* / *The boys **run**.*
- *Each / every / everyone / nobody* → singular: *Everyone **is** here.*
- *Ravi and Sita* → plural: *Ravi and Sita **are** here.*
- Ignore words in between: *The box of pencils **is** on the desk.* (the box is)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *I am having a cold* — fine in Indian English speech, but in standard writing prefer *I have a cold*. Verbs like *know, like, want, have (own)* are rarely used with -ing: *I know* not *I am knowing*.
- *He don't* ❌ → *He doesn't* ✅

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Look out of a window and write 3 present-continuous sentences. Then write 2 sentences about things you have done this year.

activity.prompt: Choose the right verb form.
activity.text: Look! It ___ (rain). Yesterday at 6 p.m. we ___ (watch) TV. I ___ (finish) my project, so I can play now. Everyone ___ (be) ready. The box of chalks ___ (be) empty.

quiz.q: When the bell rang, the children ___ .

scenes.text: Rahul in Kanpur reads 'The magician made the coin **disappear** — it was **unbelievable**!'
He doesn't know *unbelievable*, but he spots **un-**, **believe** and **-able**.
'Not able to be believed!' he says.
Then his British friend Olivia says, 'It's **raining cats and dogs**.' Rahul runs to the window to look for cats! An idiom isn't meant literally.

steps.title: Prefixes (at the start)
steps.body:
- **un-** = not: *unhappy, unkind*
- **dis-** = not/opposite: *disagree, dishonest*
- **re-** = again: *redo, rewrite*
- **pre-** = before: *preview, prepaid*
- **mis-** = wrongly: *misspell, misunderstand*
- **im-/in-** = not: *impossible, incorrect*

steps.title: Suffixes (at the end)
steps.body:
- **-ful** = full of: *careful, joyful*
- **-less** = without: *careless, homeless*
- **-able** = can be: *readable, washable*
- **-er / -or** = person who: *teacher, actor*
- **-ly** = in that way: *quickly, kindly*
- **-ness** = state of: *kindness, darkness*

steps.title: Taking words apart
steps.body:
*un + help + ful* → **unhelpful** = not full of help.
*re + use + able* → **reusable** = can be used again.
Spelling note: *happy + ness* → *happiness* (y → i).

steps.title: Common idioms
steps.body:
- *Raining cats and dogs* — raining very heavily
- *A piece of cake* — very easy
- *Break the ice* — start a friendly conversation
- *Once in a blue moon* — very rarely
- *Under the weather* — feeling unwell
- *Hit the books* — study hard

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *mispell* ❌ → *misspell* ✅ (mis + spell)
- *unpossible* ❌ → *impossible* ✅
- Using idioms in formal writing too often; they suit stories and conversation.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make 5 new words from 'kind': unkind, kindness, kindly, unkindness, kind-hearted. Use one idiom in a sentence about your week.

activity.prompt: Match each idiom with its meaning.

quiz.q: 'The test was a piece of cake' means…

scenes.text: In Kozhikode, Class 5 reads an original poem by their classmate Nila:
*The clouds roll in like elephants grey, / They trumpet thunder and block the day. / The rain is a drummer on every roof, / And puddles are mirrors — here is the proof!*
Ms Pillai asks: 'Which lines rhyme? How are clouds like elephants?'
The class discovers that poems use sound and pictures to make us feel.

steps.title: Rhyme and rhythm
steps.body:
**Rhyme**: words that end with the same sound — *grey / day, roof / proof*. A **rhyme scheme** labels rhyming lines with letters: here **AABB**.

**Rhythm** is the beat you feel when you read aloud. Clap along to hear it.

steps.title: Simile and metaphor
steps.body:
- **Simile** compares using **like** or **as**: *clouds roll in **like elephants***, *as brave as a lion*.
- **Metaphor** says something **is** something else: *the rain **is a drummer***, *puddles **are mirrors***.

Both help us **see** a picture in our minds.

steps.title: Sound words and personification
steps.body:
- **Onomatopoeia**: words that sound like their meaning — *buzz, splash, crash, drip*.
- **Personification**: giving human actions to things — *the clouds **trumpet** thunder*, *the wind **whispered***.

steps.title: Reading a poem aloud
steps.body: Read slowly, pause at commas and line ends, change your voice for feeling. Read it twice: once for the sound, once for the meaning. Ask: what picture do I see? How does it make me feel?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking every poem must rhyme — many good poems don't.
- Calling 'as brave as a lion' a metaphor: it uses **as**, so it is a simile.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a 4-line poem about summer with one simile and one rhyming pair.

statements.s: 'The clouds roll in like elephants' is a simile.
'The rain is a drummer' is a simile.
statements.why: No 'like' or 'as' — it is a metaphor.
Free verse poems do not rhyme.
It sounds like what it means.

quiz.q: 'The wind whispered secrets' is an example of…
quiz.why: Wind is given a human action.

scenes.text: A children's magazine announces a story competition. Arnav in Dehradun has an idea about a lost dog in the hills.
His first try jumps from 'Once upon a time' to 'They lived happily ever after' in 3 lines.
His older cousin Grace teaches him the **story mountain**: beginning, build-up, problem, climax, ending.
Arnav plans, writes, edits — and his story is printed in the magazine!

steps.title: The story mountain
steps.body:
1. **Beginning** — who, where, when. *On a foggy morning in Mussoorie, Tara walked her dog, Biscuit.*
2. **Build-up** — something starts. *Biscuit chased a monkey off the path.*
3. **Problem** — things go wrong. *Biscuit disappeared into the forest.*
4. **Climax** — the most exciting moment. *Tara heard barking from a steep slope…*
5. **Ending** — how it is solved and how characters feel. *With a forest guard's help, she carried him home, muddy and happy.*

steps.title: Characters and setting
steps.body: Give your main character a **name**, a **want** and a **feeling**. Describe the **setting** with senses: *the pine trees dripped, the air smelled of wet earth*.

steps.title: Show, don't tell
steps.body:
Tell: *Tara was scared.*
Show: *Tara's hands shook and her heart thumped as she called Biscuit's name again and again.*

Use **dialogue** with speech marks: *"Biscuit, where are you?" Tara shouted.* Start a new line for each new speaker.

steps.title: Edit like an author
steps.body: After writing, read aloud. Check: Does it make sense? Is the order clear? Did I use paragraphs? Are capitals, full stops and speech marks right? Can I replace a dull word (*went, said, nice*) with a better one (*raced, whispered, glorious*)?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'It was all a dream' endings — they can feel like a cheat.
- Too many characters for a short story. Two or three is plenty.
- No problem = no story. Something must go wrong.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Put the story mountain steps in order below, then write your own 5-paragraph story.

activity.prompt: Put the parts of the story in the right order.
items: Beginning: Tara walks Biscuit on a foggy morning in Mussoorie.
Build-up: Biscuit chases a monkey off the path.
Problem: Biscuit disappears into the forest.
Climax: Tara hears barking from a steep slope and finds a forest guard.
Ending: They bring Biscuit home safely; Tara promises to use a leash.

quiz.q: What is the climax of a story?
quiz.why: The top of the story mountain.

options: He slammed the door and his face turned red.

quiz.why: A problem makes the story move.

quiz.q: Which is the best setting description?
options: Mist curled between tall pines and the path smelled of wet earth.

'The moon is a silver plate' is a…

Learners can say and recognise the व्यंजन from क to ह and the joined letters क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ, श्र

scenes.text: दिल्ली में छह साल की पिहू हिंदी सीख रही है। उसकी दोस्त एमा (Emma) जर्मनी से आई है और वह भी सीखना चाहती है।
दीदी कहती हैं: 'अ से अनार, आ से आम!'
पिहू जोड़ती है: 'इ से इमली, ई से ईख, उ से उल्लू!'
एमा हँसती है: 'Every vowel has a picture-word. Now I can remember!'

steps.title: स्वर क्या हैं? (What are swar?)
steps.body:
**स्वर** वे अक्षर हैं जिन्हें हम बिना किसी दूसरे अक्षर की मदद के बोल सकते हैं।

हिंदी में 11 स्वर हैं: **अ आ इ ई उ ऊ ऋ ए ऐ ओ औ**

इनके साथ **अं** (anusvar) और **अः** (visarga) भी पढ़े जाते हैं।

*Swar are vowels — sounds you can say on their own.*
steps.say: स्वर: अ आ इ ई उ ऊ ऋ ए ऐ ओ औ

steps.title: चित्र-शब्द (Picture words)
steps.body:
- **अ** — अनार (pomegranate)
- **आ** — आम (mango)
- **इ** — इमली (tamarind)
- **ई** — ईख (sugarcane)
- **उ** — उल्लू (owl)
- **ऊ** — ऊन (wool)
- **ऋ** — ऋषि (sage)
- **ए** — एड़ी (heel)
- **ऐ** — ऐनक (spectacles)
- **ओ** — ओखली (mortar)
- **औ** — औरत (woman)
- **अं** — अंगूर (grapes)

steps.title: छोटा और बड़ा (short and long)
steps.body:
कुछ स्वर जोड़ी में आते हैं — एक छोटा, एक लंबा:

- **अ** (short a) — **आ** (long aa)
- **इ** (short i) — **ई** (long ee)
- **उ** (short u) — **ऊ** (long oo)

लंबे स्वर को थोड़ा खींचकर बोलें। *Say the long vowel a little longer.*

steps.title: आम गलती (Common mistake)
steps.body: **इ** और **ई** एक जैसे दिखते हैं। ई के ऊपर एक घुमावदार रेखा होती है। **उ** और **ऊ** में भी ध्यान दें — ऊ के नीचे एक और मोड़ होता है।

steps.title: करके देखो (Try this)
steps.body: घर में ऐसी चीज़ें ढूँढो जिनका नाम किसी स्वर से शुरू हो: आम, अलमारी, इत्र, ऊन…

quiz.q: हिंदी में कितने स्वर हैं? (How many swar?)
'आम' किस स्वर से शुरू होता है?
Which is the long form of इ?

scenes.text: लखनऊ में आरव की दादी ने उसे व्यंजन सिखाने के लिए एक खेल बनाया।
हर कार्ड पर एक अक्षर और एक चित्र: क से कबूतर, ख से खरगोश, ग से गमला।
दादी कहती हैं: 'देखो, हर पंक्ति मुँह के एक हिस्से से बोली जाती है — क-ख-ग-घ गले से!'
एक हफ्ते में आरव ने सारे व्यंजन पहचान लिए।

steps.title: व्यंजन (Consonants)
steps.body:
**व्यंजन** को बोलने में स्वर की मदद लगती है — हर व्यंजन में छिपा हुआ **अ** होता है: क = क् + अ।

पाँच-पाँच के वर्ग (groups):

- **क ख ग घ ङ**
- **च छ ज झ ञ**
- **ट ठ ड ढ ण**
- **त थ द ध न**
- **प फ ब भ म**

और: **य र ल व**, **श ष स ह**

steps.title: चित्र-शब्द
steps.body: क — कबूतर · ख — खरगोश · ग — गमला · घ — घड़ी · च — चम्मच · छ — छतरी · ज — जहाज़ · झ — झंडा · ट — टमाटर · ठ — ठठेरा · ड — डमरू · ढ — ढोल · त — तितली · थ — थर्मस · द — दवात · ध — धनुष · न — नल · प — पतंग · फ — फल · ब — बत्तख · भ — भालू · म — मछली · य — यज्ञ · र — रथ · ल — लड्डू · व — वन · श — शलगम · ष — षट्कोण · स — सेब · ह — हाथी

steps.title: संयुक्त व्यंजन (Joined letters)
steps.body:
दो व्यंजन मिलकर नया अक्षर बनाते हैं:

- **क्ष** = क् + ष (क्षत्रिय, कक्षा)
- **त्र** = त् + र (त्रिशूल, पत्र)
- **ज्ञ** = ज् + ञ (ज्ञान)
- **श्र** = श् + र (श्रमिक)

steps.title: कहाँ से बोलें (Where the sound comes from)
steps.body: क-वर्ग गले से, च-वर्ग तालु (roof of mouth) से, ट-वर्ग जीभ मोड़कर, त-वर्ग दाँतों से, प-वर्ग होंठों से। हर वर्ग का दूसरा और चौथा अक्षर साँस के झोंके (breath) के साथ बोलें: क-**ख**, ग-**घ**।

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body: **ब** और **व** मिलते-जुलते हैं — ब के बीच में एक तिरछी रेखा होती है। **घ** और **ध**, **म** और **भ** को भी ध्यान से देखें।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: अपने परिवार के सदस्यों के नाम का पहला व्यंजन लिखो: मम्मी — म, पापा — प, दीदी — द।

lessons.title: बिना मात्रा के शब्द (Words without matras)

scenes.text: पटना में रिया अपने घर की चीज़ों पर पर्चियाँ चिपका रही है।
दरवाज़े के पास लिखा: **घर**। पानी के मटके पर: **जल**। फूलदान पर: **कमल**।
पापा हैरान: 'तुमने बिना किसी मात्रा के इतने शब्द लिख दिए!'
रिया: 'हर अक्षर में अ छिपा है, इसलिए ये शब्द आसानी से बन जाते हैं!'

steps.title: दो अक्षर के शब्द
steps.body:
जब हम दो व्यंजन साथ रखते हैं तो शब्द बनता है:

- **घ + र = घर** (house)
- **ज + ल = जल** (water)
- **फ + ल = फल** (fruit)
- **न + ल = नल** (tap)
- **ब + स = बस** (bus / enough)
- **क + ल = कल** (yesterday / tomorrow)

steps.title: तीन और चार अक्षर के शब्द
steps.body:
- **कमल** (lotus) = क + म + ल
- **नमक** (salt) = न + म + क
- **शहर** (city) = श + ह + र
- **बतख** (duck) = ब + त + ख
- **सड़क** (road) = स + ड़ + क
- **अजगर** (python) = अ + ज + ग + र

steps.title: छोटे वाक्य
steps.body:
- **कमल जल पर है।** (The lotus is on the water — 'पर' and 'है' are useful helper words.)
- **नल चल रहा है।**
- **बस रुक गई।**

(Some helper words like है and गई have matras — you'll learn those next!)

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body: शब्द के अक्षरों के बीच जगह मत छोड़ो: **क मल** ❌ → **कमल** ✅। पर दो शब्दों के बीच जगह ज़रूरी है: **कमलजल** ❌ → **कमल जल** ✅। शिरोरेखा (the top line) पूरे शब्द पर एक साथ खींचो।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: इन अक्षरों से कितने शब्द बना सकते हो? **म, न, क, ल, र, घ** — जैसे: मन, कल, घर, नमक, कमल।

activity.prompt: अक्षर जोड़कर शब्द लिखो (Join the letters to write the word).

scenes.text: जयपुर में स्कूल की प्रार्थना-सभा के बाद टीचर मीनू जी एक नई कविता सिखाती हैं।
बच्चे ताली बजाकर गाते हैं: 'सूरज दादा आए हैं…'
छोटा कबीर खिड़की से बाहर चिड़िया देखता है — 'वह भी गा रही है!'
सब बच्चे कविता घर जाकर अपने परिवार को सुनाते हैं।

steps.title: कविता: सूरज दादा (VidyaVerse original)
steps.body:
**सूरज दादा आए हैं,**
**किरणें सुनहरी लाए हैं।**
**चिड़िया चूँ-चूँ गाती है,**
**सबको रोज़ जगाती है।**

**फूल खिले हैं बगिया में,**
**ओस चमकती पत्तियों में।**
**उठो-उठो, अब आँखें खोलो,**
**सबसे मीठी बोली बोलो।**
steps.say: सूरज दादा आए हैं, किरणें सुनहरी लाए हैं। चिड़िया चूँ-चूँ गाती है, सबको रोज़ जगाती है।

steps.title: शब्दों के अर्थ (Word meanings)
steps.body:
- **किरणें** — rays
- **सुनहरी** — golden
- **बगिया** — little garden
- **ओस** — dew
- **बोली** — way of speaking / words

steps.title: तुक वाले शब्द (Rhyming words)
steps.body: कविता में आख़िरी शब्द मिलते-जुलते हैं: **आए — लाए**, **गाती — जगाती**, **खोलो — बोलो**। इन्हें **तुकांत शब्द** कहते हैं।

steps.title: कविता कैसे सुनाएँ
steps.body: धीरे और साफ़ बोलो, हर पंक्ति के बाद थोड़ा रुको, और चेहरे पर मुस्कान रखो। हाथों से इशारे करो: सूरज के लिए हाथ ऊपर, चिड़िया के लिए पंख।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: 'पानी' और 'रानी' की तरह तीन और तुकांत जोड़ियाँ बनाओ: नाना — गाना, मोर — शोर…

lessons.title: आ, इ, ई की मात्राएँ (aa, i, ee signs)

scenes.text: भोपाल में मीरा की दीदी कॉलेज में पढ़ती हैं। मीरा उनकी डायरी में लिखा पढ़ने की कोशिश करती है: **दीदी**।
'द के आगे यह लंबी लकीर क्या है?' मीरा पूछती है।
दीदी बताती हैं: 'यह **ई की मात्रा** है। स्वर जब व्यंजन से मिलता है, तो **मात्रा** बनकर आता है।'
मीरा तुरंत पढ़ती है: दादा, दिन, दीया!

steps.title: मात्रा क्या है? (What is a matra?)
steps.body:
जब कोई स्वर व्यंजन के साथ जुड़ता है, तो वह एक छोटे चिह्न (sign) के रूप में लिखा जाता है — इसे **मात्रा** कहते हैं।

- क + **आ** = **का** (ा)
- क + **इ** = **कि** (ि)
- क + **ई** = **की** (ी)

**अ** की कोई मात्रा नहीं होती — वह हर व्यंजन में पहले से छिपा है।

steps.title: आ की मात्रा ( ा )
steps.body: व्यंजन के **बाद** खड़ी लकीर: **माला, राजा, नाना, आम, काला, दादा, बादल, ताला**।

steps.title: इ की मात्रा ( ि ) और ई की मात्रा ( ी )
आम गलती: छोटी इ और बड़ी ई
steps.body: **दिन** (day) और **दीन** (poor/humble) — अलग शब्द, अलग अर्थ! छोटी इ को छोटा बोलो, बड़ी ई को लंबा। और याद रखो: ि की लकीर अक्षर से **पहले** आती है, भले ही आवाज़ बाद में आए।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: 'क' के साथ तीनों मात्राएँ लगाओ: का, कि, की। अब 'म' के साथ: मा, मि, मी। 'नाना', 'नानी', 'नदी' लिखो।

quiz.q: Which matra is written BEFORE the letter?
quiz.why: छोटी इ (ि) अक्षर से पहले लिखी जाती है।

quiz.q: किस अक्षर की मात्रा नहीं होती?

lessons.title: उ, ऊ, ऋ की मात्राएँ (u, oo, ri signs)

scenes.text: कोलकाता के फूल-बाज़ार में अर्जुन अपनी नानी के साथ जाता है।
दुकान पर लिखा है: **फूल**, **गुलाब**, **सूरजमुखी**।
नानी कहती हैं: 'नीचे लगने वाली मात्राएँ देखो — **ु** छोटा उ, **ू** बड़ा ऊ।'
घर लौटकर अर्जुन लिखता है: गुड़िया, भालू, कछुआ।

steps.title: उ की मात्रा ( ु )
steps.body: अक्षर के **नीचे** छोटा मोड़: **गुलाब, कुत्ता, गुड़िया, मुकुट, सुबह, चुप**।

steps.title: ऊ की मात्रा ( ू )
steps.body: अक्षर के नीचे उल्टा मोड़: **फूल, भालू, झूला, सूरज, दूध, आलू**।

steps.title: र के साथ ध्यान
steps.body: **र** के साथ ये मात्राएँ बगल में लगती हैं: **रु** (रुपया) और **रू** (रूमाल)। यह अलग दिखता है, इसलिए खास याद रखो।

steps.title: ऋ की मात्रा ( ृ )
steps.body: अक्षर के नीचे छोटा हुक: **कृपा, गृह, मृग, वृक्ष, कृषि**। (ऋ की आवाज़ हिंदी में अक्सर 'रि' जैसी बोली जाती है।)

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: अपने घर की चार चीज़ें लिखो जिनमें उ या ऊ की मात्रा हो: झाड़ू, चूल्हा, कुर्सी, तराज़ू।

activity.prompt: सही मात्रा लगाकर शब्द पूरा करो (Write the full word).

lessons.title: ए, ऐ, ओ, औ, अं और ँ

scenes.text: इंदौर में दशहरे के **मेले** में तान्या और उसका दोस्त ओमर जाते हैं।
एक बोर्ड पर लिखा है: **मिठाइयाँ** — 'ऊपर का चाँद-बिंदु क्या है?' ओमर पूछता है।
तान्या: 'यह आवाज़ को नाक से बुलवाता है — **चंद्रबिंदु**!'

steps.title: ए ( े ) और ऐ ( ै )
steps.body:
- **े** — अक्षर के ऊपर एक तिरछी लकीर: **मेला, केला, सेब, पेड़, रेल**
- **ै** — दो तिरछी लकीरें: **पैसा, बैल, मैदान, थैला, कैसे**

steps.title: ओ ( ो ) और औ ( ौ )
steps.body:
- **ो** — आ की लकीर के ऊपर एक तिरछी लकीर: **मोर, घोड़ा, खिलौना, रोटी, सोना**
- **ौ** — लकीर के ऊपर दो तिरछी लकीरें: **कौआ, औरत, नौका, चौका, मौसम**

steps.title: अनुस्वार ( ं ) और चंद्रबिंदु ( ँ )
steps.body:
- **अनुस्वार ( ं )** — ऊपर एक बिंदु, 'न/म' जैसी आवाज़: **अंगूर, पतंग, गंगा, संतरा, कंघी**
- **चंद्रबिंदु ( ँ )** — चाँद और बिंदु, आवाज़ नाक से: **चाँद, माँ, आँख, हँसना, गाँव**

जब अक्षर के ऊपर पहले से कोई मात्रा हो (जैसे ि, े, ो), तो चंद्रबिंदु की जगह अक्सर सिर्फ़ बिंदु लिखते हैं: **मैं, हैं, नहीं**।

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body: **ए/ऐ** में उलझन: **बेल** (vine / a fruit) और **बैल** (ox) — अलग अर्थ! **ओ/औ**: **सोना** (gold / to sleep) और **सौ** (hundred)।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: 'क' पर हर मात्रा लगाकर पूरी बारहखड़ी लिखो: क का कि की कु कू के कै को कौ कं कः।

cards.back: क का कि की कु कू के कै को कौ कं कः

quiz.q: 'चाँद' में ऊपर का चिह्न क्या कहलाता है?

steps.title: वाक्य क्या है?
steps.body:
शब्दों का ऐसा समूह जिससे **पूरी बात** समझ आए, **वाक्य** कहलाता है।

- **राम खाना खाता है।** ✅
- **खाना राम** ❌ (बात पूरी नहीं)

हिंदी में अक्सर क्रम होता है: **कौन + क्या/किसे + क्या करता है**: *सीता (कौन) किताब (क्या) पढ़ती है (क्या करती है)।*

steps.title: पूर्ण विराम और प्रश्नचिह्न
steps.body:
हिंदी में वाक्य के अंत में **पूर्ण विराम ( । )** लगता है — अंग्रेज़ी के full stop की तरह।

प्रश्न के अंत में **?** लगाओ: *तुम्हारा नाम क्या है?*

भाव दिखाने के लिए **!**: *वाह! कितना सुंदर!*

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body:
- *मैं खुश है* ❌ → *मैं खुश **हूँ*** ✅
- *लड़के खेल रहा है* ❌ → *लड़के खेल **रहे हैं*** ✅
- वाक्य के अंत में । लगाना मत भूलो।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: अपने बारे में पाँच वाक्य लिखो: मेरा नाम… है। मैं … कक्षा में पढ़ता/पढ़ती हूँ। मुझे … पसंद है।

scenes.text: वाराणसी के एक स्कूल में कक्षा 4 के बच्चे एक अख़बार बना रहे हैं।
अनुष्का लिखती है: 'अनुष्का ने गंगा देखी। अनुष्का को गंगा बहुत सुंदर लगी। अनुष्का ने गंगा की फ़ोटो ली।'
मास्टरजी मुस्कुराते हैं: 'इतनी बार अनुष्का? **सर्वनाम** का प्रयोग करो!'
'मैंने गंगा देखी। **मुझे** वह बहुत सुंदर लगी। **मैंने** उसकी फ़ोटो ली।'

steps.title: संज्ञा (Noun)
steps.body:
किसी **व्यक्ति, वस्तु, स्थान, प्राणी या भाव** के नाम को **संज्ञा** कहते हैं।

- व्यक्ति: अनुष्का, किसान, डॉक्टर
- स्थान: वाराणसी, स्कूल, बाज़ार
- वस्तु: किताब, कलम
- प्राणी: गाय, तोता
- भाव: खुशी, दया, ईमानदारी

steps.title: संज्ञा के तीन मुख्य भेद
steps.body:
1. **व्यक्तिवाचक** — किसी खास का नाम: *गंगा, ताजमहल, अनुष्का, दिल्ली*
2. **जातिवाचक** — पूरी जाति/वर्ग का नाम: *नदी, इमारत, लड़की, शहर*
3. **भाववाचक** — भाव या गुण, जिन्हें छू नहीं सकते: *प्यार, बचपन, मिठास, थकान*

steps.title: सर्वनाम (Pronoun)
steps.body:
संज्ञा के **स्थान पर** आने वाले शब्द **सर्वनाम** कहलाते हैं: **मैं, हम, तुम, आप, वह, वे, यह, ये, कोई, कौन, अपना**।

*सीमा बाज़ार गई। **वह** फल लाई।* — 'वह' सीमा के स्थान पर आया।

steps.title: आदर में 'आप'
steps.body: बड़ों, शिक्षकों और अनजान लोगों से **आप** कहकर बात करो: *आप कैसे हैं?* दोस्तों से **तुम**।

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body: भाववाचक संज्ञा को विशेषण से न मिलाओ: **मीठा** (विशेषण — कैसा?) पर **मिठास** (भाववाचक संज्ञा)। **बच्चा** जातिवाचक, **बचपन** भाववाचक।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: अपनी कक्षा की पाँच व्यक्तिवाचक और पाँच जातिवाचक संज्ञाएँ लिखो।

scenes.text: मकर संक्रांति पर अहमदाबाद की छत पर हेतल और उसका भाई जय पतंग उड़ा रहे हैं।
जय: '**लाल** पतंग **ऊँची** उड़ रही है! वह **बड़ी** पतंग **कट गई**!'
हेतल हँसती है: 'तुम तो विशेषण और क्रिया साथ-साथ बोल रहे हो!'
शाम को दोनों ने अपनी डायरी में **दस** विशेषण और **दस** क्रियाएँ लिखीं।

steps.title: विशेषण (Adjective)
steps.body:
संज्ञा या सर्वनाम की **विशेषता** (कैसा? कितना? कौन-सा?) बताने वाले शब्द **विशेषण** हैं।

- गुण: **लाल** पतंग, **ईमानदार** लड़का, **मीठा** आम
- संख्या: **दो** किताबें, **पहला** इनाम
- मात्रा: **थोड़ा** दूध, **दो लीटर** पानी

जिसकी विशेषता बताई जाए, उसे **विशेष्य** कहते हैं: *लाल **पतंग*** — पतंग विशेष्य।

steps.title: क्रिया (Verb)
steps.body:
जिन शब्दों से **काम का करना या होना** पता चले, वे **क्रिया** हैं: **खाना, दौड़ना, पढ़ना, उड़ना, सोना, हँसना**।

*बच्चे **खेल रहे हैं**।* *पतंग **कट गई**।*

क्रिया का मूल रूप **-ना** पर ख़त्म होता है: पढ़**ना**, लिख**ना**।

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body: क्रिया को संज्ञा के लिंग के अनुसार बदलना ज़रूरी है: *लड़की पढ़ता है* ❌ → *लड़की **पढ़ती** है* ✅।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: अपनी माँ या पापा के सुबह के पाँच काम लिखो — हर वाक्य में क्रिया को रेखांकित करो।

scenes.text: चंडीगढ़ में बारिश के दिन गुरप्रीत, उसकी कज़िन सारा (लंदन से) और नानी शब्दों का खेल खेलते हैं।
नानी: 'राजा का स्त्रीलिंग?' गुरप्रीत: 'रानी!'
सारा: 'किताब — many?' गुरप्रीत: 'किताबें!'
नानी: 'और सूरज के दूसरे नाम?' — 'रवि, दिनकर, भानु!' सब ताली बजाते हैं।

steps.title: लिंग (Gender)
steps.body:
हिंदी में हर संज्ञा **पुल्लिंग** (masculine) या **स्त्रीलिंग** (feminine) होती है — चीज़ों की भी!

- लड़का → लड़की, राजा → रानी, शेर → शेरनी, घोड़ा → घोड़ी, मोर → मोरनी, बेटा → बेटी, अध्यापक → अध्यापिका
- चीज़ें: *किताब* (स्त्रीलिंग — किताब अच्छी है), *पेड़* (पुल्लिंग — पेड़ बड़ा है)

steps.title: वचन (Number)
steps.body:
**एकवचन** (एक) और **बहुवचन** (अनेक):

- लड़का → लड़के, कमरा → कमरे
- किताब → किताबें, बहन → बहनें
- लड़की → लड़कियाँ, नदी → नदियाँ
- कुछ शब्द वैसे ही रहते हैं: *घर → घर, फल → फल* (क्रिया से पता चलता है: फल पका है / फल पके हैं)

steps.title: पर्यायवाची (Synonyms)
steps.body:
- **सूरज** — रवि, दिनकर, भानु, सूर्य
- **पानी** — जल, नीर, अंबु
- **पेड़** — वृक्ष, तरु
- **माँ** — माता, जननी
- **घर** — गृह, भवन, मकान

steps.title: विलोम (Opposites)
steps.body: दिन ↔ रात, सुख ↔ दुख, अमीर ↔ ग़रीब, आगे ↔ पीछे, सच ↔ झूठ, ऊपर ↔ नीचे, जीत ↔ हार, प्रश्न ↔ उत्तर, आना ↔ जाना

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body: *मेरी घर* ❌ → *मेरा घर* ✅ (घर पुल्लिंग)। *मेरा किताब* ❌ → *मेरी किताब* ✅। चीज़ों का लिंग पढ़ते-सुनते हुए याद करो।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: दस चीज़ों के नाम लिखो और उनके साथ 'मेरा' या 'मेरी' लगाओ: मेरी कुर्सी, मेरा बस्ता…

activity.prompt: विलोम शब्द मिलाओ (Match the opposites).

scenes.text: बेंगलुरु में रहने वाली दस साल की तारा की दादी प्रयागराज में रहती हैं।
दादी कहती हैं: 'फ़ोन तो ठीक है, पर एक चिट्ठी लिखो — मैं उसे संभालकर रखूँगी।'
तारा पत्र लिखती है: स्थान, तारीख़, 'आदरणीय दादीजी', अपनी खबरें, और अंत में 'आपकी प्यारी पोती'।
दादी चिट्ठी पढ़कर बहुत खुश होती हैं और जवाब में अपनी बचपन की कहानी लिखती हैं।

steps.title: अनुच्छेद (Paragraph)
steps.body:
एक विषय पर कुछ वाक्यों का समूह **अनुच्छेद** है।

- **पहला वाक्य** विषय बताए: *मेरा प्रिय त्योहार दीवाली है।*
- **बीच के वाक्य** कारण और विवरण दें: *हम घर साफ़ करते हैं, दीये जलाते हैं, रंगोली बनाते हैं…*
- **आख़िरी वाक्य** बात पूरी करे: *इसीलिए मुझे दीवाली सबसे अच्छी लगती है।*

steps.title: अनौपचारिक पत्र का ढाँचा (Informal letter)
steps.body:
1. **स्थान और तारीख़** (ऊपर बाईं ओर): *बेंगलुरु, 12 मार्च*
2. **संबोधन**: *आदरणीय दादीजी,* / *प्रिय मित्र राहुल,*
3. **अभिवादन**: *सादर प्रणाम।* / *नमस्ते।*
4. **मुख्य बात**: अपनी खबर, प्रश्न
5. **समापन**: *बाकी सबको मेरा प्रणाम कहिएगा। पत्र का उत्तर जल्दी दीजिएगा।*
6. **अंत**: *आपकी प्यारी पोती, तारा*

steps.title: एक नमूना पत्र
steps.body:
*बेंगलुरु, 12 मार्च*

*आदरणीय दादीजी,*
*सादर प्रणाम। मैं यहाँ ठीक हूँ और आशा करती हूँ कि आप भी स्वस्थ होंगी। पिछले हफ़्ते हमारे स्कूल में विज्ञान-प्रदर्शनी थी। मैंने पानी बचाने पर एक मॉडल बनाया और मुझे दूसरा इनाम मिला। गर्मी की छुट्टियों में हम आपसे मिलने आएँगे।*
*आपकी प्यारी पोती,*
*तारा*

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body:
- बड़ों को पत्र में 'तुम' मत लिखो — 'आप' लिखो।
- संबोधन के बाद अल्पविराम ( , ) लगाओ।
- एक ही बात बार-बार न दोहराओ।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: अपने किसी मित्र को अपनी छुट्टियों के बारे में एक छोटा पत्र लिखो। नीचे दी गई सूची से जाँचो।

scenes.text: देहरादून में कक्षा 5 के बच्चे स्कूल के पुराने नीम के पेड़ के नीचे बैठते हैं।
शिक्षिका रश्मि जी एक कविता पढ़ती हैं — 'मैं हूँ पेड़…'
आदित्य पूछता है: 'पेड़ बोल कैसे सकता है?' रश्मि जी: 'कविता में चीज़ें इंसानों की तरह बोल सकती हैं — इसे **मानवीकरण** कहते हैं।'
उस दिन बच्चों ने स्कूल में दस नए पौधे लगाए।

steps.title: कविता: मैं हूँ पेड़ (VidyaVerse original)
steps.body:
**मैं हूँ पेड़, खड़ा हूँ कब से,**
**धूप-हवा सब सहता हूँ।**
**छाया देता, फल भी देता,**
**फिर भी चुप ही रहता हूँ।**

**चिड़ियों का घर मेरी डाली,**
**साँसें देती मेरी हरियाली।**
**मुझको काटो मत, ओ भैया,**
**मैं ही धरती की खुशहाली।**

steps.title: कठिन शब्दों के अर्थ
steps.body:
- **सहता** — सहन करता (endures)
- **छाया** — छाँव (shade)
- **डाली** — शाखा (branch)
- **हरियाली** — हरापन, पेड़-पौधे (greenery)
- **खुशहाली** — सुख-समृद्धि (well-being, prosperity)

steps.title: भाव (Meaning)
steps.body: पेड़ खुद अपनी कहानी सुना रहा है। वह धूप-हवा सहकर भी हमें छाया, फल और साँस लेने के लिए हवा देता है, चिड़ियों को घर देता है। कवि कहता है — पेड़ मत काटो, क्योंकि पेड़ धरती की खुशहाली हैं।

steps.title: कविता की बातें
steps.body:
- **तुक**: सहता — रहता, डाली — हरियाली — खुशहाली
- **मानवीकरण**: पेड़ इंसान की तरह बोल रहा है।
- **संदेश**: पर्यावरण की रक्षा।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: किसी नदी, बादल या पहाड़ की ओर से चार पंक्तियाँ लिखो — जैसे वह खुद बोल रहा हो।

courses.title: Class 1 Maths: Numbers, adding & shapes
courses.summary: Count, read and write numbers up to 100, add and take away within 20 using objects and a number line, and spot shapes and patterns all around you.
outcomes: Learners can count, read and write numbers 1–100 and say which is bigger
Learners can add two numbers with a total up to 20
Learners can take away within 20 and check by adding back
Learners can name circles, triangles, squares and rectangles and continue a pattern

scenes.text: Riya's grandmother in Ratnagiri brings a basket of mangoes. 'How many?' she asks.
Riya starts counting one by one: 1, 2, 3… she loses count at 14 and has to start again!
Dadi smiles: 'Make bundles of ten.' Riya puts the mangoes in rows of ten.
Two full rows of ten and 3 extra. 'Twenty-three!' Riya shouts. Counting in tens is faster and safer.

steps.title: Counting means one number for one thing
steps.body:
When we count, we touch **one object** and say **one number**. Never skip an object and never touch the same object twice.

- Move each counted thing to one side, so you know it is done.
- The **last number** you say tells you **how many** there are.
steps.say: When we count, we touch one object and say one number.

steps.title: Tens and ones
steps.body:
After 9 comes 10. Ten ones make **one ten**.

- 23 means **2 tens and 3 ones**.
- 40 means **4 tens and 0 ones**.
- 100 means **ten tens** — one hundred.

So when you see a 2-digit number, the left digit tells how many tens and the right digit tells how many ones.

steps.title: Bigger or smaller?
steps.body:
To compare two numbers, first look at the **tens**. More tens means a bigger number: 41 is bigger than 38 because 4 tens is more than 3 tens.

If the tens are the same, look at the **ones**: 56 is bigger than 52.

We can also say: the number that comes **after** is bigger. 30 comes after 29, so 30 > 29.

steps.title: Number words
steps.body:
Learn to read and write number names: one, two, three… ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen… twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, hundred.

Twenty-one is written with a little line (hyphen) between the two words.

steps.title: Common mistake: writing 31 for 13
steps.body: Thirteen is **1 ten and 3 ones** → 13. Children often write 31 because they hear 'three' first. Say it slowly: thir-**teen** means 3 more than **ten**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Count the steps on your stairs, the spoons in your kitchen or the buttons on your shirt. Then say the number before and the number after.

activity.prompt: Tap each mango once and count aloud. How many mangoes are there?

quiz.why: After 59 comes 60 — the ones go back to 0 and we get one more ten.
41 has 4 tens; 38 has only 3 tens, so 41 is bigger.

scenes.text: Kabir in Patna has 8 marbles. His friend Lucy from London, visiting her aunt, gives him 5 more.
'How many now?' Kabir counts all of them from 1 again — it takes a long time.
His sister shows a trick: start at 8 in your head, then count on 5 more: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13.
'Thirteen marbles!' Counting on from the bigger number is quick.

steps.title: What adding means
steps.body:
**Adding** means putting things together to find **how many in all**. The sign **+** is read 'plus', and **=** means 'is the same as'.

3 + 2 = 5 means 3 things and 2 more things together make 5 things.

steps.title: Count on along a number line
steps.body:
To find 8 + 5:

- Put your finger on **8**.
- Make **5 jumps** forward: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13.
- You land on **13**. So 8 + 5 = 13.

Always start from the **bigger** number — fewer jumps, fewer mistakes.

steps.title: Make ten first
steps.body:
Ten is a friendly number. For 9 + 6, take 1 from 6 to make 9 into 10. Now it is 10 + 5 = **15**.

Pairs that make 10: 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6, 5+5. Learn them by heart — they help with everything later.

steps.title: Order does not matter
steps.body: 3 + 5 and 5 + 3 both make 8. When you add, you can swap the numbers. Adding 0 changes nothing: 7 + 0 = 7.

steps.title: Common mistake: counting the start number
steps.body: When counting on from 8, do **not** say '8' as your first jump. The first jump lands on 9. If you count 8 again, your answer will be one too small.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take two handfuls of dry beans or stones. Count each handful, write an adding sentence like 6 + 7 = 13, then count all of them to check.

activity.prompt: Fill in the missing numbers.

quiz.q: Meena has 4 pencils and gets 0 more. How many?

quiz.why: Order does not matter in adding.

scenes.text: Amma makes 15 laddoos for Diwali in Chennai.
Arjun and his cousins eat 6 of them before the guests arrive!
'How many are left for the guests?' Amma asks.
Arjun counts back from 15: 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 9. 'Nine left!' Then he checks: 9 + 6 = 15. Correct.

steps.title: What subtracting means
steps.body:
**Subtracting** (taking away) means finding **how many are left** or **how many more**. The sign **−** is read 'minus'.

15 − 6 = 9 means: start with 15, take 6 away, 9 are left.

steps.title: Count back on a number line
steps.body: For 15 − 6: put your finger on 15 and make **6 jumps back**: 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 9. You land on **9**.

steps.title: Finding the difference
steps.body: Rohan has 12 stickers, Sara has 8. How many more does Rohan have? Count **up** from 8 to 12: 9, 10, 11, 12 → 4 jumps. So 12 − 8 = **4**. Counting up works well when the numbers are close.

steps.title: Check with adding
steps.body: Subtraction and addition are partners. If 15 − 6 = 9, then 9 + 6 must equal 15. Always check your answer this way.

steps.title: Common mistake: swapping the numbers
steps.body: In subtraction, order **matters**. 9 − 4 = 5, but 4 − 9 does not work with whole things — you cannot take 9 apples from 4 apples. Always start with the bigger (starting) amount.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Put 10 spoons on the table. Hide some under a cloth. Ask someone to work out how many are hidden by counting the ones left.

statements.why: Taking away nothing leaves the same number.

quiz.why: Count back 6 from 15 to land on 9.

quiz.q: Rohan has 12 stickers and Sara has 8. How many more does Rohan have?

quiz.why: The answer plus the amount taken away gives the start number.

quiz.q: There were 10 birds; 3 flew away. Which sum tells how many stayed?

scenes.text: Zoya and her friend Mateo walk to the market in Jaipur.
'The wheel of that rickshaw is a circle,' says Mateo.
Zoya points at a samosa: 'A triangle!' The window is a rectangle, a carrom board is a square.
At the cloth shop they see a border: red, blue, red, blue… 'That's a pattern,' says the shopkeeper. 'It repeats.'

steps.title: Flat shapes
steps.body:
- **Circle** — perfectly round, no corners, no straight sides (a bangle, a roti).
- **Triangle** — 3 straight sides and 3 corners (a samosa, a road sign).
- **Square** — 4 equal straight sides and 4 square corners (a carrom board).
- **Rectangle** — 4 straight sides and 4 square corners; opposite sides equal (a door, a book).

steps.title: Solid shapes
steps.body: Real things are solid. A ball is a **sphere**, a dice is a **cube**, a matchbox is a **cuboid**, an ice-cream cone is a **cone**, a pipe or a tin is a **cylinder**. A sphere rolls; a cube slides; a cylinder can do both.

steps.title: Patterns repeat
steps.body:
A pattern is something that **repeats in the same order**. 🔴🔵🔴🔵🔴… next comes 🔵.

Numbers make patterns too: 2, 4, 6, 8, … (add 2 each time) → next is 10. 5, 10, 15, … → next is 20.

steps.title: Common mistake: a tilted square
steps.body: A square turned on its corner (like a diamond ◆) is **still a square**. Turning a shape does not change its name. Count its sides and check they are equal.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Go on a shape hunt at home. Find 2 circles, 2 rectangles and 1 triangle. Then make a pattern with spoons and forks: spoon, fork, fork, spoon, fork, fork…

activity.prompt: Sort each thing by its shape.

items.text: A slice of sandwich cut corner to corner

quiz.why: A circle is round with no corners.
Red, blue repeats, so after red comes blue.

quiz.q: A dice is shaped like a…
quiz.why: A dice has 6 equal square faces: a cube.

questions.why: 6 and 4 is a pair that makes 10.
76 has 7 tens and 6 ones; 70 has 7 tens and 0 ones.

questions.q: A shape has 4 equal sides and 4 square corners. It is a…
questions.why: Four equal sides and square corners make a square.

Which sum is NOT equal to 12?
Ten tens and five more make…

questions.why: Difference is 6; if Mia gives 3 to Ravi, both have 12.

scenes.text: In Kolkata, Tara helps her uncle pack beads. Beads come in strings of 10, and boxes of 10 strings.
One box holds 10 strings of 10 = 100 beads.
An order says 'two hundred and forty-six beads'. Tara packs 2 boxes, 4 strings and 6 loose beads.
Uncle checks: 200 + 40 + 6 = 246. 'Perfect packing!'

steps.title: Each place has a value
steps.body:
In a 3-digit number, each digit lives in a **place**:

- the right place is **Ones** (O)
- the middle place is **Tens** (T)
- the left place is **Hundreds** (H)

In **246**, the 2 means 2 hundreds = 200, the 4 means 4 tens = 40, the 6 means 6 ones = 6.

steps.title: Expanded form
steps.body:
Writing a number as a sum of its places is called **expanded form**.

- 246 = 200 + 40 + 6
- 509 = 500 + 0 + 9 (no tens — the **0 holds the place**)
- 870 = 800 + 70 + 0

steps.title: Comparing 3-digit numbers
steps.body:
Compare **hundreds first**, then tens, then ones.

- 412 vs 398 → 4 hundreds > 3 hundreds, so **412 > 398**.
- 563 vs 571 → hundreds same, 6 tens < 7 tens, so **563 < 571**.

The open mouth of > or < always faces the bigger number.

steps.title: Common mistake: forgetting the zero
steps.body: 'Five hundred and nine' is **509**, not 59 or 5009. Each place must be filled; if there are no tens, write 0 in the tens place.

steps.title: Ordering numbers
steps.body: Smallest 3-digit number: **100**. Biggest 3-digit number: **999**. One more than 999 is **1000** (one thousand).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Using the digits 3, 7 and 1 once each, make the biggest number (731) and the smallest number (137). Try with your own three digits.

activity.prompt: Match each number to its expanded form.

quiz.q: In 583, what is the value of 8?
quiz.why: 8 is in the tens place: 8 tens = 80.
999; one more makes 1000, which has 4 digits.

scenes.text: At a school fair in Pune, the Class 2 stall sells 47 paper boats in the morning and 38 in the afternoon.
Ishaan adds: 7 + 8 = 15. 'I can't write 15 in one place!'
Ms Fernandes explains: write 5 and **carry** the 1 ten to the tens column.
4 + 3 + 1 = 8 tens. Total: 85 boats sold!

steps.title: Line up the places
steps.body: Write numbers one under the other so **ones are under ones** and **tens under tens**. Always start adding from the **ones** column (right side).

steps.title: Adding with carrying: 47 + 38
steps.body:
- Ones: 7 + 8 = 15 → write **5**, carry **1** ten.
- Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 (carried) = **8**.
- Answer: **85**.

Why carry? Because 15 ones = 1 ten and 5 ones, and a place can hold only one digit.

steps.title: Subtracting with borrowing: 52 − 27
steps.body:
- Ones: 2 − 7 is not possible with whole things, so **borrow** 1 ten from the 5 tens. Now there are 4 tens and 12 ones.
- Ones: 12 − 7 = **5**.
- Tens: 4 − 2 = **2**.
- Answer: **25**. Check: 25 + 27 = 52 ✓

steps.title: Common mistake: subtracting the smaller digit from the bigger
steps.body: In 52 − 27, some children do 7 − 2 = 5 in the ones column. That is wrong — the top number's ones (2) must have 7 taken from it, so you must borrow. Always take the **bottom** digit from the **top** digit.

steps.title: Word problems: which operation?
steps.body:
- 'In all', 'altogether', 'total' → usually **add**.
- 'Left', 'how many more', 'difference', 'fewer' → usually **subtract**.

But always picture the story; words are clues, not rules.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Solve 365 + 128 the same way: ones 5 + 8 = 13 (write 3, carry 1), tens 6 + 2 + 1 = 9, hundreds 3 + 1 = 4 → **493**.

activity.prompt: A bus had 64 passengers. At a stop, 28 got off. How many are still on the bus?

quiz.why: 'How many are left' means take away.

scenes.text: For a community puja in Bhubaneswar, chairs are set in 4 rows with 5 chairs in each row.
Neel counts: 5, 10, 15, 20. 'Twenty chairs!'
His father says: that is **4 times 5**, written 4 × 5 = 20.
Later, 3 friends get 2 sweets each: 2 + 2 + 2 = 3 × 2 = 6 sweets.

steps.title: Multiplication is repeated adding
steps.body:
When the **same number** is added again and again, we can multiply.

5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = **4 × 5** = 20. Read '4 times 5' or '4 fives'. The sign is **×**.

steps.title: Arrays show multiplication
steps.body:
Rows and columns are called an **array**. 3 rows of 4 dots = 3 × 4 = 12.

Turn the array sideways and you get 4 rows of 3 = 4 × 3 = 12. So **3 × 4 = 4 × 3** — order does not change the answer.

steps.title: Tricks
steps.body:
- Anything × 1 = itself. Anything × 0 = 0.
- ×10: just put a 0 at the end (7 × 10 = 70).
- ×4 is **double, then double again**: 4 × 6 → 12 → 24.

steps.title: Common mistake: adding instead of multiplying
steps.body: 3 × 4 is **not** 3 + 4 = 7. It means 3 groups of 4 = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Draw the groups if unsure.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Count shoes at home in 2s, fingers in 5s and toes on 4 people in 10s. Say the matching table aloud.

quiz.why: Order does not matter in multiplying.
Put a 0 at the end of 8.

quiz.q: A spider has 8 legs. How many legs do 2 spiders have?

scenes.text: Aanya goes to a mela in Lucknow with ₹50: one ₹20 note, two ₹10 notes, one ₹5 coin and five ₹1 coins.
She wants a kulfi for ₹15 and a balloon for ₹20.
15 + 20 = ₹35. She has ₹50, so she can buy both and get ₹15 back.
Her friend Leo, visiting from Canada where people use dollars, learns that India's money is the **rupee (₹)**.

steps.title: Coins and notes
steps.body:
India's money is the **rupee**, written **₹**. You will see coins of ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 and ₹20, and notes of ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200 and ₹500.

1 rupee = 100 **paise**. Small paise coins are rarely used in shops today, but you will meet paise again in decimals.

steps.title: Adding up a bill
steps.body: Kulfi ₹15 + balloon ₹20 = **₹35**. Add money just like numbers, then write ₹ in front.

steps.title: Giving change
steps.body:
Aanya pays ₹50 for a ₹35 bill. Change = 50 − 35 = **₹15**.

Shopkeepers often **count up**: 35 → 40 (₹5 coin) → 50 (₹10 note). ₹5 + ₹10 = ₹15.

steps.title: Many ways to make the same amount
steps.body: ₹20 can be one ₹20 note, or two ₹10s, or four ₹5s, or ₹10 + ₹5 + ₹5. Value matters, not the number of coins: three ₹1 coins are worth less than one ₹5 coin.

steps.title: Stay safe with money
steps.body: Keep money in a safe pocket, count your change in front of the shopkeeper, and never show your money to strangers.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Play shop at home: price 5 things (₹8, ₹12, ₹25…), use paper notes and practise giving change from ₹50.
